articles.title: Brit Hume: Republican ‘washout’ possible in midterms
articles.summary: Fox News’s Brit Hume on Wednesday said Republicans may face rough results in the upcoming midterms. “Republicans have to worry that something like that may happen to them in this race, where not only do they lose the close ones, but they lose a lot that weren’t even thought to be close, and you’ve got…
articles.body:
Fox News’s Brit Hume on Wednesday said Republicans may face rough results in the upcoming midterms.

“Republicans have to worry that something like that may happen to them in this race, where not only do they lose the close ones, but they lose a lot that weren’t even thought to be close, and you’ve got a big washout,” Hume said when asked by Fox News’s Bret Baier on “Special Report” about the upcoming election, while discussing prior elections in which Republicans saw widespread success.

“I’m not saying it’s going to happen, but I think it could happen,” he added.

Republicans are facing an uphill battle this election cycle, facing issues like the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s slumping approval ratings and concerns about the cost of living. Democrats have also been leading their GOP opponents in recent polls.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 38.7 percent on Thursday afternoon, while his disapproval rating was 59.4 percent .

Energy costs have also risen as a result of the Iran war, during which the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, has been closed. According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was about $4.33, up from about $3.07 last year .

On Wednesday, Republican political operative Rick Tyler said the GOP was facing “a lot of problems” going into the midterms.

In an appearance on “CNN News Central,” Tyler noted tight midterm races in Alaska, Michigan, Iowa and Ohio.

“It’s going to be a bad night for Republicans,” Tyler said, referring to Election Day. “It just is. How bad? We don’t know.”

articles.title: Secret documents reveal donors behind $330 million for Trump’s ballroom
articles.summary: A list obtained by The Washington Post reveals all the major donors to President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project, including previously undisclose...
articles.body:
A list obtained by The Washington Post reveals all the major donors to President Donald Trump's White House ballroom project, including previously undisclosed contributors who have benefited from regulatory decisions, government contracts and, in one case, a pardon for a family member.

Tech giants Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million, the top contribution amount, the list shows. The Adelson family, one of the GOP's largest donor dynasties, committed that sum as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network.

Absent from the list is Trump himself, who has said that he is helping to pay for the project. "It's being paid for a hundred percent by me and some friends of mine," he said last year, days after demolition began on the old East Wing.

The White House publicly identified 37 people, companies and foundations as donors last October, without revealing the amount of their individual gifts.

The list obtained by The Post, an internal spreadsheet used to track contributions for the fundraising effort, contains the source, date and amount of all 67 donations above $10,000 recorded as of late last month. It shows a total of $333 million from private donors, aligning with the administration's public statements. Additional records, also internal to the fundraising effort, provide more detail about the donations and indicate that at least $77 million came from donors who requested anonymity.

The list and other documents offer a panoramic view of a fundraising campaign that is extraordinary both for its size and opacity. Ordinary political giving requires public disclosure and is subject to campaign finance rules. The ballroom donations are collected by a nonprofit and then channeled to the government and into a White House account the president directly controls.

Independent experts and scholars have expressed alarm at the potential the arrangement has for influence buying and coerced giving.

Some donors on the list obtained by The Post cut large checks, while others created installment plans that are still being paid off, the additional records show. The list does not include in-kind contributions.

The Post's reporting does not establish a connection between the donation commitments and favorable actions by the Trump administration. But the documents show that the vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government.

Companies or executives of firms that have had contracts with the federal government during Trump's second term accounted for about half of the total, The Post found.

After reviewing the list obtained by The Post, White House spokesman Davis Ingle declined to discuss individual donations but described the ballroom donors as "a wide array of great American companies and generous individuals, all of whom are contributing to make the People's House better for generations to come."

"The same critics who are alleging fake conflicts of interests, would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue renovations," he said. He added that the administration will "relentlessly pursue those responsible for this cowardly leak while continuing to protect all those who give."

The Post is publishing the names of the 57 donors listed as having committed to giving $100,000 or more. The additional records detailing donors' preferences show at least nine wanted to remain anonymous.

The Post attempted to reach all the donors whose names appear in this report. Most did not respond or declined to comment. Those who did comment said that there was no connection between their donations and any favorable government actions.

Nvidia, the world's most valuable public company, became a top contributor to the ballroom in October 2025, nearly three months after it struck a groundbreaking pact with Trump to sell advanced microchips to China despite national security concerns.

CEO Jensen Huang told reporters at the time that the company was contributing to Trump's ballroom "in a small way" but did not provide a dollar amount. Documents show Nvidia requested that its $25 million donation be kept anonymous.

"As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said in response to questions from The Post. "We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made."

Major GOP donor Joseph Popolo Jr., Trump's ambassador to the Netherlands, and his wife contributed $1 million from their family fund to support the ballroom project in late 2025, the records show. Their donation - made two months after Popolo's confirmation - has not been previously reported.

Trump Cabinet member Kelly Loeffler of the Small Business Administration and her husband Jeff Sprecher, former chairman of the New York Stock Exchange, promised $5 million for the project, the list shows. Brandon Lutnick, chairman of investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald and the son of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, donated stock worth more than $2.5 million, the records show.

Popolo, Loeffler, Sprecher and the Lutnicks did not respond to requests for comment.

More than three-quarters of the money for the ballroom came in commitments of $5 million or more. Among the top donors are some of America's blue-chip companies, including Amazon, Caterpillar, Comcast, Microsoft and T-Mobile. (Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos owns The Post . )

Cryptocurrency companies, now under loosened regulations from the Trump administration, and their investors promised more than $18 million. The largest portion came from Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss, co-founders of the Gemini crypto exchange, who together donated bitcoin valued at $5,050,018, the records show.

The Winklevoss brothers did not respond to requests for comment.

The ballroom project has also received dozens of small contributions, some as low as $10. The list and additional documents show the source of all but $24,000 of the total donations.

The total fundraising amount falls short of the $400 million Trump has said he intends to raise for the work. The cost of building the new East Wing, which includes the ballroom, office space and an underground military facility, was projected in March to have increased to $600 million, an estimate previously reported by The Post. The White House has used taxpayer dollars to cover some of the construction cost, records show.

The ballroom donations are routed through the Trust for the National Mall, a D.C.-based nonprofit whose mission is to restore and preserve the National Mall and the White House grounds. Nonprofits are not generally required to disclose their donors.

Prospective donors were sent a "pledge agreement form," a copy of which was obtained by The Post, for giving toward the "Donald J. Trump Ballroom." The form lists Meredith O'Rourke, the top fundraiser for Trump's 2024 campaign, as the main contact.

O'Rourke referred questions to the White House.

A 12-page agreement between the government and the Trust requires that the Trust "maintain the anonymity of Project donors to the extent provided by law and not publicly recognize any such donor unless explicitly authorized in writing" by staff in the White House's Executive Residence unit.

Democratic lawmakers have denounced the fundraising for the ballroom as secretive and potentially transactional. They have demanded that the administration and the Trust provide details about the donors and circumstances of the gifts. Those demands have been rebuffed.

In a statement the Trust said: "In philanthropy, it is not uncommon for donors to request their gifts remain anonymous. The Trust is committed to honoring donors requesting anonymity."

One of the earliest commitments to donate to the ballroom, from Sept. 23, 2025, came from the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini, an international banker and dual Venezuelan-Italian citizen.

In 2022, the Justice Department indicted Herrera Velutini, then 50, on bribery charges, accusing him of helping finance the campaign of Puerto Rico's then-governor in exchange for the removal of a regulator investigating his bank. The former governor and a political consultant were also charged.

Herrera Velutini and his attorney unsuccessfully tried to get the case dismissed, claiming prosecutors were criminalizing lawful political activity.

After Trump's victory, Herrera's daughter, Isabela Herrera, made two donations to Trump's MAGA Inc., a political action committee, totaling $3.5 million, campaign finance records show.

The donations prompted the nonprofit Campaign Legal Center to file a complaint with the Federal Election Commission alleging that Isabela Herrera was serving as a "straw donor" for her father. The organization described her as a self-employed financial consultant in her mid-20s whose only prior political donation was $20 to Pete Buttigieg, a 2020 Democratic presidential candidate.

The organization said it got no response from the FEC, which declined to comment for this story.

In August 2025, Herrera Velutini's charges were reduced to a misdemeanor as part of a plea agreement.

The following month, Isabela Herrera committed to donating $2.5 million for the ballroom, which has not been previously reported. Records show she paid a first installment of $835,000 on Oct. 14, 2025. Trump pardoned Herrera Velutini in January. Herrera's second payment was due this month, the records show.

Amid a wider Justice Department retreat from sweeping public corruption investigations, Trump also pardoned the former governor and the political consultant. The White House said the prosecutions had been politically motivated.

After the pardon, an attorney for Herrera Velutini issued a statement saying his client was "profoundly grateful to President Donald J. Trump for bestowing the grace of his benevolent pardon."

Neither Herrera Velutini nor his daughter responded to requests for comment.

Last year, Ergen, the telecommunications executive, found his company EchoStar in the Trump administration's crosshairs.

Brendan Carr, the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, wrote Ergen in May to inform him that the agency had begun investigating EchoStar. Carr threatened to yank government licenses that were critical to the survival of the business, accusing EchoStar, owner of Dish Network, of not following through on promises it had made to upgrade its cellphone network.

The following month, Ergen met with Trump and Carr behind closed doors to discuss the investigation, according to Bloomberg. The outlet, citing unnamed sources, said the June 11 discussion included a brief exchange about Ergen's political donations and whether he gave to candidates in both political parties.

The company referenced a June 11 meeting between Ergen and Carr in a regulatory filing and wrote that Trump "subsequently encouraged the parties involved to reach an amicable resolution."

Ergen negotiated a deal to sell some of the company's licenses to AT&T in August, subject to approval of the FCC and Justice Department.

Carr dropped the investigation the following month, thanking Ergen for his responses and for information he had provided.

In December, with the sale still pending, Ergen committed $12.5 million to Trump's ballroom, according to the donation list. Records indicate Ergen requested that the source of the donation remain anonymous. The donation has not been previously reported.

He committed another $12.5 million in February, according to the list.

In May, the FCC and the Justice Department each gave EchoStar approval for the sale.

Through a spokesman, Ergen and EchoStar declined to comment. The FCC and Carr did not respond. DOJ did not provide comment for this story.

The donor list also shows $5 million "pledged" by AT&T, the only line item on the list described that way. Every other amount is listed as "won."

In a statement to The Post, AT&T spokesperson Megan Ketterer said the company appeared to have been listed in error. "We have no idea what list you are talking about and have no plans to contribute to the Trust for the National Mall," Ketterer said.

Another top donor was a subsidiary of Rocket, the Detroit-based housing, finance and tech company founded by Daniel Gilbert, owner of the NBA's Cleveland Cavaliers.

In March 2025, Rocket said that it planned to acquire two competitors: the home search site Redfin and the mortgage site Mr. Cooper. The moves would give Rocket a much larger share of the real estate market.

Federal agencies tasked with protecting against anticompetitive business practices declined to challenge the deals, allowing them to proceed. Five Democratic senators wrote to the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission in protest.

To acquire Mr. Cooper, Gilbert also needed approval from the Federal Housing Finance Agency.

The FHFA approved the deal on Aug. 26, 2025.

The Rocket subsidiary committed $10 million to the ballroom three weeks later. Records show it requested anonymity.

A Rocket spokesperson said the approvals and donation were not connected.

"Rocket and its related companies have supported the Trust for the National Mall and other nonpartisan organizations in Washington for more than a decade," said spokesperson Aaron Emerson. "We're proud to join dozens of companies and individuals in improving our nation's capital."

An FTC spokesperson said Rocket received no special treatment, pointing to a lawsuit the agency brought against Redfin for anticompetitive practices days after the donation.

The FHFA and the Justice Department did not provide comment.

One of the country's leading software providers, Salesforce, has significantly grown its government contracting business during the second Trump administration.

Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff has attended exclusive dinners and events with Trump, including a state dinner hosted by King Charles III at Windsor Castle in September 2025 and a business summit in Japan the following month. While there, Trump thanked Benioff for previously putting him on the cover of Time magazine, which Benioff owns.

"Marc has some pretty good suggestions," Trump said of the CEO.

The following day, Benioff committed $1 million to the ballroom, according to the list. The donation has not previously been reported, and Benioff asked that it remain anonymous.

Salesforce separately made two $1 million commitments to the ballroom, one last Christmas Eve and another Jan. 29 of this year, the list shows. The donations have not been previously reported.

In between, the Army awarded the company a contract worth up to $5.6 billion through 2035, which appears to be the largest public government contract in Salesforce's history, according to a review of public contracting records. Announcing the contract, the Pentagon said "bids were solicited via the internet with only one received."

Benioff and Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.

In a statement, a Pentagon official said: "Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department's funding decisions."

After this article published, an Army spokesperson said in a statement that contracts are awarded in strict compliance with federal law and are "determined exclusively by validated mission requirements, technical capability, and best value."

One of Salesforce's competitors, ServiceNow, also donated to the ballroom.

Last September, the General Services Administration announced what it called a "landmark" agreement with ServiceNow that would make the company's AI-driven software available to federal agencies at a discount.

"When President Trump says the federal government needs to operate like a best-run business, he means it," CEO Bill McDermott said as part of the announcement.

The next month, ServiceNow committed $5 million to the ballroom, a donation that has not been previously reported.

The GSA said in a statement that ServiceNow has been a federal contractor for more than a decade, adding that "its charitable or political donations - like those of any company - have no bearing on GSA's decision to include them in federal buying catalogs."

ServiceNow said in a statement that negotiations for the deal had been underway for a "considerable period of time." Its government business is "separate and unconnected to any donations we make to any cause," it said.

Of the donation, the company said: "Many of our partners and peers were also contributing to the project. We chose to join them."

Nearly $10 million for the ballroom was committed by two Trump political donors who have pursued large investments in Venezuelan oil - a market Trump has gained influence over since the U.S. seizure of President Nicolás Maduro in January.

Billionaire financier Paul Singer committed to donate $5 million through his foundation in October 2025, a month before his hedge fund received court approval to pursue a purchase of Venezuelan oil giant Citgo for $5.9 billion.

The deal will require approval from multiple federal agencies, including the Commerce Department, Energy Department, State Department and Treasury Department. It has stalled amid ongoing negotiations with the South American country's U.S.-backed administration.

The Oklahoma oil and gas company Continental Resources and its chairman emeritus, billionaire and GOP megadonor Harold Hamm, both promised donations to the ballroom in October 2025 totaling just under $5 million.

This year, in response to the Trump administration's call for energy companies to invest in the Venezuelan oil industry, Continental struck a tentative agreement with the country's state-run oil company to develop 126,000 acres of untapped oil fields.

Singer declined to comment. Neither Hamm nor Continental responded.

Two companies and one individual the White House has publicly named as donors do not appear on the list obtained by The Post.

The companies are Hard Rock International, the hospitality chain owned by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, and Tether America, a cryptocurrency firm. The individual is Paolo Tiramani, a modular homes company executive who told the Times of London that he had donated $10 million in stock.

None of the three answered The Post's questions or explained why they are not recorded as having contributed to the ballroom fundraising campaign. Neither did the Trust for the National Mall or the White House.

Kevin Crowe, Samantha Schmidt, Dan Lamothe and Alex Horton contributed to this report.

articles.title: Justice Department does not need to save records from investigations into former CIA director, court says
articles.summary: A federal judge on Thursday declined to require the Justice Department to preserve records from investigations into former CIA director John Brennan.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A federal judge on Thursday declined to issue a court order requiring the Justice Department to preserve all its records from investigations into John Brennan so the former CIA director can challenge any eventual criminal case against him as a malicious prosecution. Attorneys for Brennan conceded that the request for a court order was unusual but said it was necessary given what they called the Justice Department's pattern of vindictiveness in its pursuit of him and its recent track record of erasing or failing to preserve records. But U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb declined the request, saying Brennan's arguments were too speculative. As CIA director in the final years of President Barack Obama's Democratic administration, Brennan was a key figure in the U.S. intelligence community's conclusion that Russia had interfered in sweeping fashion in the 2016 presidential election on behalf of Republican Donald Trump, who went on to defeat Democrat Hillary Clinton for the White House. The Justice Department has not made any public accusations about Brennan, but House Republicans have referred him to the department for potential prosecution on allegations that he lied to Congress, which he has vigorously denied. Brennan has for months been entangled in Justice Department investigations into whether he made false statements to Congress in 2023 and a broader Florida-based inquiry into whether he and other former intelligence and law enforcement officials engaged in a conspiracy to keep Trump from power. He was subpoenaed to testify before a grand jury in the broader conspiracy investigation, and his lawyers have said they've been told by prosecutors that he remains a target in a separate and more discrete false-statements investigation. It is unclear whether Brennan will face charges, but attorneys for him said that they intended to challenge any prosecution on vindictive-prosecution grounds and that any records they received from the government through a court order would be helpful in backing up their argument. Cobb was nominated in 2021 by President Joe Biden, who earlier served as Obama's vice president.

images.caption: John Brennan, Former CIA Director; NBC News Senior National Security and Intelligence Analyst, appears on "Meet the Press" in Washington, D.C., Sunday, Oct. 14, 2018.

articles.title: Pentagon spokesperson: Hegseth ‘completely aligned’ with Trump nixing execution livestream
articles.summary: A spokesperson for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth stressed Thursday that the Pentagon chief is “completely aligned” with President Trump’s decision to not livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan. Trump said the planned Dec. 3 livestream execution of Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in the November 2009 attack…
articles.body:
A spokesperson for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth stressed Thursday that the Pentagon chief is “completely aligned” with President Trump’s decision to not livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan.

Trump said the planned Dec. 3 livestream execution of Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in the November 2009 attack on Fort Hood, Texas, would not move forward . He announced the reversal in a Thursday post to Truth Social.

Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said Trump and Hegseth “spoke about the decision” ahead of the Truth Social announcement, and he said the Defense secretary “supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned.”

Hegseth earlier this month made the surprising announcement that Hasan’s execution would be made public, a plan that was swiftly admonished by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. Vice President Vance also said that, while he supported the death sentence, he did not plan to view the event.

Trump in his statement blamed Hasan’s rampage on the Obama administration, calling the event a “key intelligence failure” before noting he had heard the criticism around a public execution. He said that, while Hasan deserved to be put to death, it would not be livestreamed — even as he suggested it might have deterred potential terrorists.

“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” Trump wrote.

The president added the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, should they choose to attend.

Several Republican members of the House and Senate had immediately pushed back at Hegseth’s decision to livestream Nasan’s death, arguing the focus should be on justice for the victims and their families rather than creating a public spectacle. Many lawmakers drew comparisons between the proposal and the acts of dictators.

“A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said last week, adding the planned livestream “risks feeding that appetite.”

Hasan’s rampage at the Fort Hood processing center is the deadliest mass shooting ever on a U.S. military installation.

articles.title: Zacharia says results of bar exam were ‘inconsequential’
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Thursday her California Bar exam results are “somewhat inconsequential” after reporting surfaced that showed she did not pass the examination. In an interview with the conservative outlet Real America’s Voice, Zacharia said she was planning to move to China to be with her husband who was working abroad. …
articles.body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Thursday her California Bar exam results are “somewhat inconsequential” after reporting surfaced that showed she did not pass the examination.

In an interview with the conservative outlet Real America’s Voice, Zacharia said she was planning to move to China to be with her husband who was working abroad.

“I had already pre-registered to take the bar, and I didn’t want to withdraw from that,” Zacharia said. “I was already incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I’d been long distance from for at least a year, a year and a half when you include the engagement.”

“We just said let’s take this time, and I’ll take the bar and see what happens,” she continued. “The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn’t need the bar in China.”

Zacharia’s legal credentials have come under intense scrutiny after the left-leaning newsletter Popular Information reported that Zacharia is not licensed to practice law in the U.S. or Washington, D.C.

The Wall Street Journal reported late Wednesday that Zacharia sat for the California Bar exam after she received her law degree from Pepperdine University, but she did not pass.

Zacharia said that after moving to China, she “didn’t think much of the bar results or consider that was something I needed to focus on,” noting she worked as an associate at the international division at the Chinese law firm Zhong Lun Law Firm.

“I had enough credentials, which was my law degree, to be able to be in this practice,” she said.

When asked if she plans to weigh in on legal matters as press secretary, Zacharia said she was “not hired as White House counsel.”

“For the press secretary, my job is to amplify and communicate his message, and to interact with the press, and build relationships, and strengthen relationships, and communicate clearly the message of the administration,” she said.

images.caption: Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, listens to President Trump speak to reporters at the White House in Washington, D.C. on Oct. 12, 2026.

articles.title: Zacharia ‘tracked every news hit’ to capture Trump’s attention in press secretary search
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Thursday that she tracked President Trump’s interests and intentionally discussed them in television appearances ahead of being selected for the role. “I tracked every news hit to be in accordance with what policies he was pushing for, particularly on Truth Social, since I was the senior communications adviser…
articles.body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Thursday that she tracked President Trump’s interests and intentionally discussed them in television appearances ahead of being selected for the role.

“I tracked every news hit to be in accordance with what policies he was pushing for, particularly on Truth Social, since I was the senior communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group and Truth Social,” Zacharia said Thursday in an interview on conservative cable network Real America’s Voice.

Zacharia was selected Oct. 9 after former press secretary Karoline Leavitt left the position in August to spend more time with family.

Speaking with host Jack Posobiec, Zacharia said she did not think lobbying directly for the press secretary position would be effective, instead saying she wanted to “audition” for the role.

“I am not lobbying for this job,” Zacharia said. “Why? Because my philosophy is I’m on TV enough where if he sees me and he likes me, then I will be recruited for the job.”

Zacharia, who previously lived and worked in China, specifically highlighted her comments during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the U.S. for a summit with Trump. She said she went on TV to defend the president when he was criticized for rolling out the red carpet for Xi.

“I really wanted to give context for how you do business in China and why President Trump’s approach is actually the effective way to get the deal done,” Zacharia said. “He’s actually, by showing deference to Xi Jinping, effectuating his ability to get that deal.”

“A lot of the American people don’t understand that,” she added. “The criticism of pomp and circumstance is actually, it so means you really don’t understand what happens in China, and that President Trump is after a deal for the American people … he has never deviated from being America first.”

Zacharia held her first press briefing at the White House Tuesday, drawing attention for responding to a question saying that she passed the bar exam when she moved to China. She clarified to The New York Times that she misheard the question . The Wall Street Journal then reported Thursday that Zacharia did not pass the bar exam she took in California in 2011 after graduating from law school.

images.caption: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia listens to a reporter’s question during her first press briefing at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 13, 2026.

articles.title: Noem ‘confident Ilhan Omar will finally be held accountable’
articles.summary: Kristi Noem, the former secretary of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), said she was assured that Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) would be “held accountable” if the lawmaker is found to have committed immigration fraud after federal agents raided her home Monday. Noem, whom President Trump fired in March after a tumultuous stint leading the…
articles.body:
Kristi Noem, the former secretary of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), said she was assured that Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) would be “held accountable” if the lawmaker is found to have committed immigration fraud after federal agents raided her home Monday.

Noem, whom President Trump fired in March after a tumultuous stint leading the department, said in a Thursday interview with conservative commentator Benny Johnson that she was confident Omar “will finally be held accountable for the crimes that she’s committed.”

Trump and other prominent Republican figures have levied numerous allegations against Omar over her immigration status, accusing the Somali native of marrying her brother in order to obtain U.S. citizenship — which she has denied.

When pressed about which immigration crimes she believes Omar may have committed, the former Homeland Security chief pointed to the agency’s practice of examining all familial ties to any applicant seeking citizenship.

“If you go back and find that anything could be wrong or misrepresented, that’s when it voids or cancels out their citizenship,” Noem said.

Omar and the former Homeland Security secretary have repeatedly clashed over federal immigration operations in Minnesota. Noem was in charge of the department at the height of several prominent immigration enforcement operations and subsequent protests, and during the killings of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota by Immigration and Enforcement (ICE) officers.

The lawmaker accused Noem of spreading “lies and propaganda” about ICE arrests in Minnesota, ripping the then-secretary’s claims that immigration enforcement officers were primarily targeting migrants without legal status who had harmed children.

The Trump administration last year announced it would launch a criminal investigation into Omar for alleged immigration fraud. Homeland Security Investigations agents raided the lawmaker’s Washington, D.C., home on Monday.

The Minnesota Democrat subsequently released a fundraising email focused on the investigation, calling for supporters to “Stand with Ilhan Omar.”

“Donald Trump and DHS have opened a baseless, partisan investigation into Ilhan Omar, and she needs us by her side as they escalate their attacks,” the email reads.

“Chip in whatever you can to make sure Ilhan can beat Trump and keep fighting for our progressive values in Congress.”

articles.title: Hinojosa stages empty lectern at Texas governor’s mansion amid Abbott debate snub
articles.summary: Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa (D) spoke next to an empty lectern in front of the Lone Star State’s governor’s mansion Thursday after Gov. Greg Abbott (R) did not accept her debate invitation. “I guess the governor is a no-show, which is not surprising because he has been a no-show for Texans for years,” Hinojosa…
articles.body:
Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa (D) spoke next to an empty lectern in front of the Lone Star State’s governor’s mansion Thursday after Gov. Greg Abbott (R) did not accept her debate invitation.

“I guess the governor is a no-show, which is not surprising because he has been a no-show for Texans for years,” Hinojosa said after Abbott did not appear at the event.

The Democratic nominee accused the governor of shutting down the street in front of the executive residence where she originally planned to host the debate.

“If Greg Abbott’s not man enough to debate me then he doesn’t deserve to be the governor of Texas,” Hinojosa told the crowd.

Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long slammed the Republican governor for his refusal to debate the Democratic challenger in a statement Thursday afternoon.

“The contrast in this race could not be more clear,” Long said. “Gina Hinojosa is traveling the state, hosting more than 150 public events and meeting directly with thousands of voters in their homes and in their communities. The only people who seem to have access to Greg Abbott are the billionaire donors lining his pockets.”

At one point during the Thursday event, independent gubernatorial candidate Jenn Mack took the stage and stood behind the second lectern, according to a video clip shared online by a local Fox 7 Austin reporter.

“You came to debate Abbott on his record, and I came to debate both of you on your records,” Mack said, eliciting loud boos from the crowd.

Mack was later escorted away from the podium by an officer and another man.

Abbott’s campaign criticized this moment in a social media post , sharing a video of Mack’s removal from the stage.

“The misogyny shown toward a candidate who came to debate proves how insincere and hypocritical Gina Hinojosa is,” the campaign said in a statement.

Additionally, the Republican’s reelection campaign accused the event of not being a “sincere attempt to debate,” pointing to the fact that the empty lectern — a standing podium only reachable by stairs — was inaccessible to Abbott, who uses a wheelchair.

In a statement to The Hill, Hinojosa’s campaign spokesperson Tommy Kubitschek noted the Democratic candidate had agreed to four other debates with news outlets, while her Republican candidate hadn’t accepted any debate invitations.

Kubitschek said Hinojosa’s campaign gave Abbott a week to accept Thursday’s debate challenge outside of the governor’s mansion but received no response from his campaign.

“This was an entirely sincere attempt to allow Texans to hear two different plans for the state’s future, and Abbott has had every opportunity a candidate could hope for to engage in good faith discussion,” he said.

During a campaign stop Thursday in Tyler, Abbott defended his decision not to debate his Democratic challenger.

“The most important thing that a governor can do is to show up in communities,” the Republican said, according to the Houston Chronicle. “What voters want to see and hear, they want to see their governor in their community. They want to have the ability to ask their governor questions.”

Another Texas candidate, Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico, has similarly faced barriers in getting his Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, to meet him on the debate stage.

On Wednesday evening, Talarico participated in a town hall in Fort Worth hosted by CNN and Jubilee. CNN said they extended a similar offer to Paxton but had not heard back from the Republican’s campaign.

Polling shows both Talarico and Hinojosa locked in competitive races against their Republican opponents. Abbott is running for a fourth term in the Texas governor’s mansion.

A Marist University poll released Wednesday showed Abbott with a 4-point advantage among likely Texas voters — a lead that fell within the survey’s margin of error. In the same poll, 47 percent of respondents backed Talarico, while 45 percent supported Paxton in the Senate contest.

images.caption: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), left; and Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee in the Texas governor’s race.

articles.title: Fort Hood survivors praise Trump for scrapping Hasan execution livestream: ‘We’re not barbaric’
articles.summary: Alonzo Lunsford, shot seven times by Nidal Hasan, called Trump's decision to cancel the firing squad livestream a "positive move" for the nation.
articles.body: Survivors of the 2009 Fort Hood massacre praised President Donald Trump's decision not to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, after warning that broadcasting his death could turn the execution into a spectacle and hand terrorist groups a propaganda tool. Hasan is still set to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, 2026, and Trump said the immediate families of his victims will be permitted to witness the execution in person. But it will no longer be broadcast to the general public as previously announced by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times by Hasan during the attack nearly 17 years ago, told Fox News Digital that Trump's decision is a "positive move." "It proves that we are a better people, a better nation, and that we're not barbaric," Lunsford said in immediate reaction to the walk-back by Trump on Thursday. "We don't glorify such actions." VETERAN SHOT 7 TIMES IN FORT HOOD MASSACRE HAS A WARNING FOR AMERICANS PLANNING TO WATCH EXECUTION Lunsford said he supports Hasan's death sentence and execution by firing squad but drew a line at broadcasting it to the public. "For it to be made a spectacle for everyone to witness how they're gonna do a tailgate or, 'Hey, we're gonna have a cookout and we're gonna watch this man be put to death.' No, it's not about that," Lunsford said. "It's not a spectacle. It's not a pay-per-view event or a WWE wrestling match or even a boxing match." He also warned that footage of Hasan's execution could be seized upon by terrorist organizations. "You don't want that to be used as a tool for ISIS or al-Qaeda to recruit and say, 'Hey, this is what happens to you if you do this against the infidel,'" Lunsford said. Julia Wilson was a civilian employee at Fort Hood when Hasan went on his rampage. She was nine months pregnant during the attack, which was carried out on her due date. FORT HOOD SHOOTER SHOULD BE EXECUTED '13 TIMES OVER' — BUT NOT ON LIVE STREAM, SURVIVOR SAYS She was slammed against a wall amid the chaos of the shooting and has said that it was only by the grace of God that she and her then-unborn son survived. Wilson was already against the livestreaming of Hasan's execution because she didn't want others to be traumatized like she was during the deadly attack. "I'm ecstatic about that," she told Fox News Digital, reacting to the news that the plan to livestream the event would not proceed. "I'm worried about other people's mental health," she continued. "I don't think the government… really put a lot of thought into how this was going to go down and how it was going to transpire until today." "I don't think they really thought about how this may affect people," said Wilson. "Seeing something like that affects your mental health. I don't care who you are. I don't care what you've seen. Seeing someone murdered in front of you or killed in front of you affects your mental health, whether they deserve it or not." Wilson also worried that if the livestream had proceeded, it would exist online forever, and that children might discover it while searching the web. "Once it's on out there, it's out there," she said. "I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump continued. "That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" "We knew this guy had issues," Lunsford said. "If you are privy to the ticking time bomb report, you will see what he was talking about. This guy had issues and they just passed the buck and moved him from Walter Reed to Fort Hood." Lunsford wondered what might have happened had Hasan deployed overseas before carrying out an attack. "Suppose he would have did the deed once he got in country on a FOB, a forward operating base," he said. "Imagine how many American lives would have been lost then." For Lunsford, allowing victims to witness Hasan's execution remains important even without a public broadcast. "It's gonna be a traumatic thing for, at least for the families of the fallen," he said. "They'll be able to close the chapter and hopefully close the book." articles.body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who made headlines for her rocky debut at the podium this week, has a certain Hollywood star in mind to portray her on the NBC sketch comedy show “Saturday Night Live” (“SNL”).

“Maybe a Scarlett Johansson-type character,” she said in an interview with conservative commentator Jack Posobiec.

Johansson has hosted “SNL” numerous times and has made several guest appearances. She is married to Colin Jost, who co-anchors the show’s “Weekend Update” segment and has been a staff writer for more than two decades.

Zacharia acknowledged that the comedy show will likely parody her on its cold open sketch, as it has done numerous times in the past mocking President Trump and members of his administration, including former press secretary Karoline Leavitt.

When asked if she would watch the skit if it were to air, Trump’s new top spokesperson told Posobiec that she is “not watching anything right now.”

“I do not want to see any of the other X or Instagram or TV right now,” she said.

Her 14-minute debut behind the White House podium Tuesday drew scrutiny over her seemingly nervous demeanor, prompting speculation that “SNL” may already have enough content to parody the new press secretary in her first week on the job.

Zacharia, who was described as an “attorney” by the president and has claimed numerous times to be a lawyer, came under fire when she was asked where she took the bar exam and responded twice with “when I moved to China.”

While Zacharia did move to China after completing her law degree at Pepperdine University, there is no evidence that she ever passed the bar exam to be able to legally call herself an attorney.

Zacharia later told The New York Times that she misheard the question about her legal credentials over the noise of Marine One jets and respecting protocol by keeping her distance behind the president and away from the reporters.

“I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” she said.

articles.title: White House's Katie Zacharia confirms she never passed bar exam
articles.summary: The White House described Katie Zacharia as "uniquely qualified" to be the new press secretary.
articles.body:
Washington — White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Thursday that she never passed the bar, although she's called herself a lawyer and President Trump has referred to her as an attorney.

Zacharia made the comment in an interview with conservative commentator Jack Posobiec after the Wall Street Journal reported that she failed the bar exam in California in 2011 and did not pass the bar in any other U.S. state in which she's lived. Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University's law school.

Zacharia told Posobiec she took the bar exam in California but didn't pass, saying she was distracted by her plans to get married and move to China for her husband's work around the same time. She said she "didn't think much" of the results, and said she didn't need to pass the exam to do her work in China.

Zacharia also said she never described herself as an "attorney at law," and said there's a "lot of misinformation around the fact that I labeled myself a lawyer." She said she consulted with multiple experts.

"I was very careful how I executed this. I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law," Zacharia said.

Earlier this week, as President Trump was departing for a trip to Alaska, when reporters asked her where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia responded, "I went to China," sparking confusion about her law background.

A White House official said Zacharia earned her juris doctor from Pepperdine, which the university confirmed to CBS News. The White House official said Zacharia then moved to China with her husband for his job at an American private equity firm, while she worked on international transaction law.

Zacharia told CBS News in a statement Thursday she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," although it's not clear which credentials she meant. Only Chinese nationals may take the bar exam in China.

On Fox News in April, Zacharia said she "lived in Beijing as a corporate lawyer for three years."

Zacharia's Instagram bio also says that she is a lawyer. On Truth Social, Mr. Trump called her "a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University, and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney."

But whether it's true that she can say she's an attorney or lawyer is being disputed — and it's a question Zacharia has considered. She told The New York Times that as she was beginning to appear on cable news, she talked with Pepperdine's president about how she could describe herself. The Times said, "She said she was warned not to use the words 'attorney" or 'esquire,' but that 'lawyer' was OK."

But CNN on Thursday reported that Zacharia shared at least 15 social media posts identifying herself as an "attorney" over the last two years.

The White House said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified" for the White House press secretary role.

"Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement to CBS News. "She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary."

On Wednesday, the Campaign for Accountability, a liberal nonprofit watchdog, filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, questioning whether she had violated California law in referring to herself as a lawyer without having passed the bar. She had been living in California with her family until she became White House press secretary.

The Campaign for Accountability pointed to California Business and Professions Code Section 6126 , which says, "Any person advertising or holding himself or herself out as practicing or entitled to practice law or otherwise practicing law who is not an active licensee of the State Bar, or otherwise authorized pursuant to statute or court rule to practice law in this state at the time of doing so, is guilty of a misdemeanor."

"Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie," Campaign for Accountability executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a statement. "In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has."

Cheung blasted the left-leaning ethics group.

"This group that filed the 'complaint' is a radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome," Cheung posted to X . "Nobody takes them seriously because they are deranged low lifes."

Nora Freeman Engstron, a law professor at Stanford Law School, said the language in California's law isn't ambiguous or unclear.

"California law is crystal clear: You can't hold yourself out as a lawyer unless you're authorized to practice law," she told CBS News. "And the law doesn't just prohibit the unauthorized practice of law. It also prohibits the unauthorized pretense of being a lawyer."

"California law doesn't just prohibit people from practicing law without a license," she added. "It also prohibits them from pretending they're entitled to practice law. You don't have to set foot in a courtroom or represent a single client to run afoul of the statute."

articles.title: ICE tactics spark debate before pivotal US midterm elections
articles.summary: Polls have found that Trump’s hardline immigration enforcement effort has divided voters before the 2026 midterm race.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump’s mandate for aggressive immigration enforcement has fractured public support in advance of next month’s critical midterm elections.

In the lead-up to the November 3 vote, Fox News released a poll that found 53 percent of registered voters felt the immigration crackdown had “gone too far”.

That rate was even higher among demographics that may be key to the Republican Party’s prospects in November.

The poll, conducted in September, found that 60 percent of independent voters agreed with the idea that Trump’s immigration efforts have overreached. Two-thirds of Hispanic participants also agreed with the campaign having “gone too far”.

Experts say the political debate about immigration in the US has shifted since the last major election in 2024. At the time, the focus was largely on border security. But increasingly, attention has fallen on how enforcement operations are being conducted.

Cynthia Penaloza is among those questioning the Trump administration’s tactics.

In August, her sister, 23-year-old Joceline Penaloza Magana, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Houston, Texas, during a traffic stop. Joceline remains in custody to this day.

“We’re always afraid. We’re uncertain of what’s going to happen, if she’s going to be sent back to Mexico, if we’re ever going to be together again or how this is going to change our lives forever,” Cynthia told Al Jazeera correspondent Phil Lavelle.

She rejects Trump’s assertion that his administration’s immigration enforcement operations have targeted “the worst of the worst”.

Joceline, according to the Penaloza family, was an honour roll student who does not have a criminal record. She was brought to the US as a young child, about five years old.

“She’s always been a good girl,” Cynthia told Lavelle.

Still, the Trump administration has tied its campaign of mass deportation to efforts to control crime.

In a statement earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees immigration enforcement, credited Trump’s policies with having “unleashed ICE to target the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens, including pedophiles, murderers, gang members, terrorists, and rapists”.

Immigration arrests have been on the rise under Trump. In September, ICE announced it had tallied two consecutive months with more than 50,000 immigration arrests, beating a record set in June, when 43,900 people were detained.

Homeland Security has argued that approximately 70 percent of its immigration detainees are criminals, if pending charges are factored in.

But critics have questioned that statistic, given that the legal system in the US gives suspects the presumption of innocence until they are proven guilty in a court of law.

In other words, many of the accused could be acquitted or see their charges dropped. A large portion of those with criminal charges may also be accused of non-violent crimes.

Analysts have found that a majority of people currently in immigration custody are not considered criminals under the law. According to the Deportation Data Project, which analyses government data sets, some 70 percent of those held in ICE detention have no criminal record.

The Trump administration has nevertheless pushed to increase detentions.

“We need more. We need more arrests, and we need more deportations,” Tom Homan, the White House “border czar”, said in an interview in July.

The aggressive arrest tactics may have repercussions on the Republican campaign for the midterms, though.

Republicans are hoping to defend their majorities in both chambers of Congress, as well as in key state and local elections.

Trump made significant gains in the 2024 elections with Hispanic voters. During his re-election bid, he received nearly 48 percent support among Latinos, according to an exit poll from the Pew Research Center — up 12 percentage points from the 2020 election.

But Pew found that his gains may be eroding. Among the Hispanic voters who supported him in 2024, his approval rating has steadily declined, from a high of 93 percent at the start of 2025 to a low of 57 percent as of last week.

Some Republicans running in the midterm election, including Congress member Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, have even openly criticised the president’s hardline immigration policies.

“Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in an advertisement campaign launched in September. She cited the large number of immigrants who were arrested without a criminal record.

Other Republicans, however, blame previous presidencies for creating the conflict over immigration enforcement.

“A mess was created, and now cleaning it up is dirty business,” Jeremy Price, a Republican in Texas, told Al Jazeera. “You’re having to find people, arrest them against their will and remove them from the country because they don’t want to leave.”

Democrats, meanwhile, hope to convert that outrage over immigration enforcement tactics into votes, come November.

“I would hope they’d abolish ICE,” Richard Gonzales, the chair of the Hidalgo County Democratic Party in Texas, said in an interview with Al Jazeera’s Lavelle.

“I mean, in my perspective, I think that they’ve, the agency has just lost its identity, and there’s no way to rehabilitate that.”

articles.body:
What does Trump’s Russia deal actually mean?

President Trump’s controversial diesel deal with Russia may not actually bring down prices ahead of the midterms.

Trump announced last week that Russia would “immediately” supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global marketplace, with another 500,000 tons coming in November, drawing howls from Democrats and some Republicans over lifting sanctions on Moscow amid its war with Ukraine.

The president added that Russia would supply another “1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” and, depending on the condition of its refineries, 3 million tons in a “short period of time.”

However, the 300,000 and 500,000 figures appear not to exceed the monthly amounts that Russia is already exporting.

According to data from Kpler , Russia exported about 141,000 barrels per day in September and 178,000 barrels per day so far in October. A calculator from CME Group shows that comes to 584,000 metric tons per month in September and 722,000 metric tons per month in October.

“These are the volumes that would have gone to the global market anyway without any additional effort,” said Tatiana Mitrova, global fellow at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy.

And, experts said, even if this many additional barrels were added to the market, it would be unlikely to actually make a dent in costs inside the U.S.

“The announced Russian diesel volumes are a small fraction, less than 5%, of US diesel demand over the next few months, so they should have very limited impact on US retail prices,” said Isabelle Gilks, principal analyst for retail fuels at Wood Mackenzie, in a statement shared with The Hill.

“The much bigger influence on prices is the constraint on supply. Russian exports have collapsed as Ukrainian drone attacks have taken refining capacity offline, and Middle East export routes remain disrupted. Unless the attacks stop and those routes reopen, there is little extra diesel to bring to market, just as winter demand picks up,” Gilks added.

Andy Lipow, president of consulting firm Lipow Oil Associates, expressed a similar sentiment last week, telling The Hill the figures are “quite small” compared with the global market’s 28 million barrels per day.

Welcome to The Hill’s Energy & Environment newsletter, I’m Rachel Frazin — keeping you up to speed on the policies impacting everything from oil and gas to new supply chains.

How policy will affect the energy and environment sectors now and in the future:

Five House Republicans signed on to a letter Thursday urging President Trump to cancel the Russian diesel deal he announced last week.

Senate Democrats demanded answers Thursday from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin about an agency study to detect the abortion pill mifepristone in drinking water.

Producer prices rose by 1.3 percent from August to September, the largest jump in more than four years, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

Nine former FBI agents sued the Justice Department on Thursday, alleging they were wrongly fired solely because of their work investigating President Trump in the Mar-a-Lago documents case.

Attorneys for the agents write that their “fate was sealed by virtue of simply having worked on an investigation into Trump’s wrongdoing,” noting Attorney General Todd Blanche has boasted of having “cleaned house” of anyone who worked on the criminal probes of the president.

The suit notes the timing of the firings, which were carried out over the course of two days as FBI Director Kash Patel was under significant scrutiny over videos that showed him partying in Italy with the U.S. men’s hockey team following their Winter Olympics win.

“Plaintiffs were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President’s personal vendetta. The firings did not follow any internal investigation or disciplinary process within the FBI, and Plaintiffs were not given any notice, a hearing, or an opportunity to appeal. Instead, Patel claimed to rely solely upon ‘Article II’ to support the firings,” the lawsuit states.

Article II is the portion of the Constitution establishing the presidency, and the White House has fired numerous individuals citing only the president’s authority.

“An ‘Article II’ firing is an invention of the current Administration. Its invocation represents an attempt to convert all federal employees into political appointees and condition their continued employment on their (perceived) personal and political loyalty to President Trump. In reality, the ‘Article II’ rationale is nothing more than a pretext for firings—like those of the Plaintiffs—that are politically retributive and unlawful,” the attorneys write.

The suit was brought on behalf of Jennifer Bacon, Zach Feldman, Gilbert Granados, Catherine Herrera, Harrison Kaufman, Jeremy Linton, Erin Matanic, Danielle Ray and Rachel Vaccaro.

The suit notes that each of the agents was assigned to the case and had worked on other high-profile investigations, including the Boston Marathon bombing and the attempted assassination of Trump in Butler County, Pa.

After a search of his Florida estate, Trump was found to have more than 300 documents with classified markings on them.

He ultimately faced Espionage Act charges for unlawfully retaining the records as well as an obstruction of justice charge after prosecutors alleged Trump demanded the documents be moved around the property to hide them from authorities and his own attorney.

The suit makes other allegations about Patel, noting the U.S invaded Iran shortly after his Olympic visit.

“Patel’s conduct in Italy in the week leading up to the war suggests he was not a central part of any planning within the Executive Branch for the national security consequences of the conflict. This scandal proved politically perilous for Patel: he drew widespread criticism for his conduct, with numerous sources suggesting that his status with President Trump and position as Director of the FBI were in jeopardy as a result,” the suit states.

It goes on to say Patel apparently violated a gag order in place in the Mar-a-Lago case by giving information about the Mar-a-Lago investigation to Reuters about subpoenas made for phone records, and then fired each of the nine defendants.

“In the article, three unnamed FBI ‘sources’ linked the Plaintiffs’ terminations to the ‘revelations’ about the phone records subpoenas in the classified documents case,” the suit states.

articles.title: CNN legal analyst: Biden-era inquiry into Omar hurts her case against Trump
articles.summary: CNN anchor Jake Tapper questioned whether Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) should have come forward about any potential issues with her immigration status during the Biden administration rather than face a criminal investigation under President Trump. Federal agents raided Omar’s Washington, D.C., home with a court-authorized search warrant Monday as part of a criminal investigation into…
articles.body:
CNN anchor Jake Tapper questioned whether Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) should have come forward about any potential issues with her immigration status during the Biden administration rather than face a criminal investigation under President Trump.

Federal agents raided Omar’s Washington, D.C., home with a court-authorized search warrant Monday as part of a criminal investigation into alleged immigration fraud, which she has denied.

In an interview with CNN senior legal analyst Elie Honig, Tapper suggested Omar might have been better off voluntarily disclosing any mistakes in her immigration paperwork during former President Biden’s time in office.

“If this is true, would it not have been wiser for the congresswoman to have gone to the Biden Justice Department and said, ‘This is what happened, and there was a mistake, and I’d like to come clean and pay whatever fine’?” Tapper said. “And then that way this is not left up to the Trump Justice Department?”

Honig acknowledged that Omar may have “fared better” under the Biden administration, considering she has sparred with Trump on numerous occasions over immigration policy, but said the decision would have posed a difficult legal dilemma.

He pointed to a separate investigation opened against Omar under the Biden administration in June 2024 examining her finances.

“I think that’s going to undermine any argument she may have down the line that this is politically selective and vindictive,” Honig said.

He did acknowledge, however, that Trump’s public attacks against Omar — including calling her “garbage” — could strengthen her argument that she is being targeted specifically.

“Donald Trump has given her plenty of ammo to argue that she’s being singled out for personal reasons,” the legal analyst noted.

The White House announced last year it would launch a criminal investigation into Omar, a Somali native, to examine whether she committed fraud in obtaining U.S. citizenship.

Authorities seized the Minnesota Democrat’s phone during a search of her home Monday and issued grand jury subpoenas to several relatives including her sister, Sahra Noor, according to reports.

Other reports stated investigators are determining whether Omar misrepresented her age on immigration documents, which could affect whether she was eligible to obtain citizenship through her father as a minor.

Trump and other GOP figures have levied numerous allegations of immigration fraud against Omar, including claims that she married her brother to help him immigrate into the country.

Omar, who became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia with her family as a child, has repeatedly denied allegations of immigration fraud, and accused the administration of being politically motivated in its efforts to deport her.

The investigation comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections, where Omar is seeking reelection in Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District.

articles.title: Why AOC was in a deep-red part of Michigan: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign swing with Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed today was about much more than boosting him on Election Day in November.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen digs into Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign trip to Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. Plus, Allan Smith rounds up the battleground Republican candidates who are distancing themselves from President Donald Trump’s tariffs. — Adam Wollner Why AOC was in a deep-red part of Michigan Analysis by Jonathan Allen Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign swing with Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed today was about much more than boosting him on Election Day in November. It was about all the Election Days after that, too. As a leader in the socialist-inspired wing of the Democratic Party, and one who is weighing a bid for the presidency, Ocasio-Cortez is eager to find evidence for the case that progressives are as good as centrists at persuading swing voters to pick Democrats — maybe even better. It’s a counterintuitive argument and one that is central to the left’s strategy for winning primary fights — including the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028. In higher-turnout elections, party voters often reject more liberal candidates at least in part because they believe those candidates would lose to Republicans in general elections. The left hopes an El-Sayed victory would persuade the broader Democratic Party to reverse that behavior. “What we do is that we break open the entire political calculus in America — period,” Ocasio-Cortez said at a New York fundraiser this month. “Because if you can win, if Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere.” For AOC and El-Sayed today, anywhere was Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. The 320-mile-wide rural strip, most of which is closer to Duluth, Minnesota, than Detroit, has long been an emblem of rural Republican strength. By campaigning there, El-Sayed and Ocasio-Cortez want to demonstrate that they are reaching out to red-area voters and later that they were successful in winning converts. But while the UP votes reliably with Republicans at the national level, there are plenty of progressive voters. In areas dominated by one party, often the people who remain in the other party are committed to ideological orthodoxy. El-Sayed did well in the Upper Peninsula in his primary, defeating centrist Democrat Haley Stevens in all three of the counties AOC was set to visit today. Without converting a single Republican, he should be able to expect tens of thousands of votes from the region. Kamala Harris even won one of the counties AOC traveled to — Marquette — 20,866 to 17,459. Maybe El-Sayed will swipe some swing voters from the UP, but the real value of AOC’s presence is bringing out as many of those Democrats as possible. If she can do that, the left will contend that its candidates are a better bet for the party in general elections. In fact, they’re already starting to make that case before the votes are in. Some Republicans in key races break with Trump over tariffs By Allan Smith In a handful of battleground races, Republican candidates are trying to distance themselves from one of President Donald Trump’s signature policy initiatives: tariffs. So far, three GOP Senate nominees and two of the party’s picks for governor are trying to cast themselves as seeking a middle ground on what has been Trump’s marquee economic policy, particularly with the cost of living rating as a top voter concern. The battleground Senate candidates are Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, former Sen. John Sununu in New Hampshire and former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan. Rep. John James of Michigan and Pennsylvania state Treasurer Stacy Garrity have also highlighted their disagreements with Trump’s tariff policies in their gubernatorial contests. “So, of course, nobody, I don’t think, agrees with the president 100% of the time,” Garrity said at a debate last week when she was asked for specific areas of disagreement with Trump. “In fact, who agrees with anyone 100% of the time? And tariffs would be a perfect example. While some tariffs have helped manufacturers, some have not.” The maneuvering is taking place as Republican candidates across the map try to figure out where they can safely distance themselves from Trump without offending him or his dedicated base, which they must turn out to the polls next month. Trump has spent years reorienting the Republican Party from a position of supporting mostly unfettered free trade to having a protectionist bent. What makes the splits over tariffs interesting is that they’re taking place mostly in states — Michigan and Pennsylvania — that were supposed to reap some of the biggest benefits from those policies through a return of manufacturing jobs. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
