articles.title: Trump shuts down Pentagon plan for public execution: 5 takeaways
articles.summary: President Trump put an abrupt end on Thursday to questions about whether the Pentagon would really livestream the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter, former Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan. In a Truth Social post, he said the public execution could serve as a deterrent but didn’t want to subject “good and well-meaning”…
articles.body:
President Trump put an abrupt end on Thursday to questions about whether the Pentagon would really livestream the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter, former Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan.

In a Truth Social post, he said the public execution could serve as a deterrent but didn’t want to subject “good and well-meaning” people to the sight. Critics have also warned about the video becoming a tool for terrorist propaganda.

Trump had previously sent mixed signals on the livestreaming plan, and others in and around the White House — including Vice President Vance and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) — said they wouldn’t watch it.

A poll released Thursday showed Americans were overwhelmingly against the idea.

Hasan, an American-born Muslim, killed 13 people and injured 32 others when he opened fire in 2009 at Fort Hood, Texas. He said he had “switched sides” in the U.S.-Afghanistan war.

Here are five takeaways from the initial announcement and Trump’s reversal:

Hegseth made the shock announcement a week ago

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the Dec. 3 execution of Hasan would be open to the public to watch. No legal execution has ever been broadcast in the U.S., and the last public execution was more than 60 years ago.

Hegseth has long wanted “the harshest lawful punishment” for Hasan. He told reporters in September 2025 that he had asked Trump for final approval for the military execution.

“Of course, we’re going to do it at Fort Hood. We’re going to do it on a Thursday, we’re going to do it at 1 o’clock, which is when he did it, and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad,” Hegseth told Real America’s Voice on the USS Abraham Lincoln in an interview Oct. 8.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” he said.

Army rules allow for at least two media outlets to be present for the execution.

Trump issued a reversal of course Thursday, as lawmakers on both sides of the aisle urged the administration to reconsider.

Trump said that while he thinks the streaming of the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan,” “many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”

The president called Hasan a “traitor [and] very bad and evil man.”

He blamed the Obama administration for a “key intelligence failure” after investigators concluded that emails Hasan had sent were not a threat.

Trump said Hasan will die as scheduled, but only immediate family of the victims can watch in person if they choose to.

“They deserve to witness JUSTICE!” he wrote.

Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that Trump and Hegseth had spoken about the decision ahead of the president’s Truth Social post.

“The Secretary supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned,” Parnell said in a statement.

Cool responses from Trump and Vance earlier this week

The reversal came after Trump and Vance appeared openly skeptical of the plan in comments to reporters over the past week.

“We’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters earlier this week.

Axios reported Monday that Trump had privately told someone close to him that the livestream “might not happen.”

Vance told reporters last week that he wouldn’t watch it but defended the execution.

“So, whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said.

“Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it,” he added.

Hegseth stirs frustration on both sides of the aisle

The livestream idea was criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, adding to growing frustration with Hegseth.

Johnson, a key ally of the administration, said he wouldn’t watch it and that some colleagues in Congress were against the idea as well.

“The concern would be that it would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists,” Johnson said in a CBS News interview over the weekend.

“I need to tell the White House what some of my colleagues think about that, and not everybody’s in favor of the idea,” he said.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) was among a handful of Republicans who spoke out against the idea.

“There is no need to livestream any execution, including this one,” Murkowski said on the social platform X . “I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America.”

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) called on the Trump administration to remove Hegseth over the plan.

“There is no doubt that Nidal Hasan is a murderer who took the lives of 13 people and injured dozens. He should face justice for that. But a public execution? Here in the United States?” Kelly wrote in a Friday post on X.

Hegseth has also angered lawmakers on both sides of the aisle with his purge of senior Pentagon officials and top generals who don’t align with his policies against diversity, equity and inclusion and “anti-woke” policies, as well as his role as a key champion of the Iran war.

Comes as Trump touts death penalty in speeches

Trump has taken to promoting the death penalty in his remarks.

At a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, on Oct. 3, Trump said Republicans will pass the death penalty for “large-scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who ever kills a police or law enforcement official.”

Trump called the death penalty for Hasan “a very worthy way of going for him” when asked about it by reporters last week.

On Wednesday, Trump said people who leak information should be shot.

“Somebody leaked, some sleazebag. They ought to go to jail and be shot. For the rest of their life, they should be in jail,” Trump said at the rally in Bullhead City, Ariz., in an apparent reference to leaks surrounding airstrikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities.

“In my opinion, leakers should be shot. In the old days, we used to shoot leakers,” he continued. “When they leak what time you’re going to attack a country, and the reason you’re attacking is really for defense because you don’t want them to have a weapon that can blow up millions of people in one shot.”

He also said reporters are “almost as bad as a leaker.”

On Thursday, Trump said he wanted to extend the death penalty to those who kill a first responder, like “anybody that murders a firefighter going up a ladder.”

articles.summary: Five people are believed dead after an active shooting incident at a Bend, Ore. elementary school, two law enforcement officials told the Associated Press. The sources told the AP it was not clear if the shooter, who the Bend Police Department said was dead, is included among the five. The AP reported that the death…
articles.body:
Five people are believed dead after an active shooting incident at a Bend, Ore. elementary school, two law enforcement officials told the Associated Press .

The sources told the AP it was not clear if the shooter, who the Bend Police Department said was dead, is included among the five. The AP reported that the death toll was preliminary and could change.

The incident was reported at Silver Rail Elementary School.

Bend Police say the suspect was shot and killed before they arrived on the scene, “possibly by a bystander.” Law enforcement sources told the AP that the shooter was a 15 or 16-year-old male.

Police first responded to the report of an active shooter at 12:59 p.m. PDT, and were on the scene three minutes later, at 1:02 p.m.

Bend Police said law enforcement was evacuating each classroom, and transporting children to Journey Church for family reunification, around five minutes from Silver Rail Elementary School.

In a statement, Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook extended sympathy to the families and those affected.

“No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing,” Cook said. “Our immediate priorities are caring for our students and staff and assisting law enforcement and emergency responders.”

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title: CBS News faces $20M defamation lawsuit after misidentifying Maryland teenager in Reflecting Pool report
articles.summary: A Maryland teenager's $20 million defamation lawsuit claims CBS News falsely linked him to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool vandalism arrests.
articles.body: CBS News is facing a defamation lawsuit as a Maryland teenager seeks $20 million in damages, claiming he was falsely identified as a person arrested for vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool’s lining. The lawsuit, filed on Wednesday in U.S. District Court in the District of Columbia, identified the 15-year-old plaintiff simply as "JV." "He was not arrested for vandalizing it. He was not accused by law enforcement of vandalizing it. Yet CBS News broadcast and published a story to a national audience that placed JV's image alongside the assertion that five people had been arrested for vandalizing and ‘sabotaging’ the Reflecting Pool, thereby falsely portraying JV as one of the perpetrators of a highly publicized federal crime," the lawsuit stated. NORTH CAROLINA STUDENT WINS $95K AFTER SCHOOL ACCUSED HER OF VANDALIZING SPIRIT ROCK WITH CHARLIE KIRK TRIBUTE "The accusation was particularly damaging because at all times material to the allegations, the Reflecting Pool renovation and subsequent alleged vandalism of the Reflecting Pool is or has been the subject of intense national attention and political controversy," the complaint continued. "President Donald Trump frequently discusses the Reflecting Pool renovation and publicly condemned those accused of vandalism in extraordinarily harsh terms, stating that they should be ‘prosecuted to the max,’" it added. The lawsuit states that CBS "inserted" JV into the controversy and "exposed him to extreme embarrassment, humiliation, and the public condemnation" directed at the actual vandals. The lawsuit claims JV’s presence near the Reflecting Pool "was entirely unrelated to the vandalism" and he was simply briefly detained for riding an e-bike in the area. NEW YORK TIMES LOSES DEFAMATION SUIT, ORDERED TO PAY $9.25M TO FORMER ALABAMA BASKETBALL PLAYER JV was released without charges and "his detention had nothing whatsoever to do with vandalism or sabotage of the Reflecting Pool." "CBS nevertheless used video footage of JV's detention in its report about the Reflecting Pool vandalism. As CBS anchor Jericka Duncan told viewers that ‘five people have been arrested,' the video depicted JV in handcuffs," the lawsuit stated. "In the version CBS distributed online and through social media, CBS showed JV turning toward the camera with his face fully visible as Duncan made the statement concerning the arrests and then identified one of the alleged perpetrators, David Hearn," it continued. "The visual and verbal presentation published by Defendants unmistakably conveyed the false message that JV was among the persons arrested for vandalizing the Reflecting Pool and further confused JV with Hearn, an adult who was subsequently indicted on a felony charge arising from the vandalism," the complaint added. JV’s legal team claimed CBS was aware that the 15-year-old was detained for the e-bike, and not vandalism, because the original video obtained by the network clearly distinguished between the two issues. "The facts alleged herein demonstrate that CBS either knew its portrayal of JV was false or acted with reckless disregard for whether it was true," the lawsuit alleged. "CBS compounded the harm through the manner and breadth of its publication," it continued. "Although the national television broadcast did not show JV's face, CBS's online and social-media version did. It showed his face immediately after depicting his distinctive sweatshirt and while reporting that arrests had been made. JV was readily recognized by friends and acquaintances." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The lawsuit pointed out that video of the report accumulated at least 1.8 million views on social media alone. JV’s legal team said he has faced "profound" consequences, including embarrassment, humiliation, anxiety, loss of sleep, emotional distress, friends distancing themselves and a continued "fear that CBS's false accusation will follow him through high school and affect his college admissions, athletic opportunities, employment, and future career." The lawsuit noted that CBS issued an on-air correction but said the "belated acknowledgment … cannot undo the publication or erase its consequences." CBS News declined comment on pending litigation. A judge permanently dismissed the Reflecting Pool vandalism case against former Olympian David Hearn, who was accused of damaging the costly $14 million renovation project in June. articles.title: Musk bankrolls PAC spending big on Paxton in Texas
articles.summary: Tech mogul Elon Musk poured $158 million into a key super PAC backing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) Senate run as part of his push to keep Republican majorities in Congress. Musk was the single donor to Texas PAC — a political action committee backing Paxton’s run — in the third quarter, according to…
articles.body:
Tech mogul Elon Musk poured $158 million into a key super PAC backing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) Senate run as part of his push to keep Republican majorities in Congress.

Musk was the single donor to Texas PAC — a political action committee backing Paxton’s run — in the third quarter, according to new federal election filings. The Texas Republican is in a razor-thin race with Democrat James Talarico for the Senate seat currently held by GOP Sen. John Cornyn.

Federal Election Commission filings show Musk gave $75 million on Sept. 9 to the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), which then disbursed the cash to Texas PAC the following day.

On Sept. 23, Musk gave another $83 million to SLF, which disbursed the same amount to Texas PAC on Sept. 24, records showed. The SLF is backed by Senate Republican leadership.

Axios first reported of the disbursements from SLF to Texas PAC.

The Musk-backed America PAC has also spent $7.5 million so far this year to support Paxton and oppose Talarico, per new filings.

Musk has various ties to Texas, managing several business ventures in the Lone Star State.

Starbase, the SpaceX industrial complex, is located in Texas and became an incorporated city last year. Musk’s tunnel company, The Boring Company, is based in San Antonio, and he is also developing a semiconductor and AI compute facility in Grimes County, Texas.

Despite previously suggesting he would pull back his political involvement, Musk is the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterms.

The New York Times previously reported the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has given about $366 million in total this cycle.

“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” America PAC spokesperson Andrew Romeo said in a statement to the Times, which was confirmed by The Hill earlier this week.

“These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” Romeo added.

The Hill’s Caroline Vakil and Sophia Vento contributed reporting.

articles.title: 4 GOP senators join letter demanding Pentagon inspector general investigation of Ukraine’s Starlink outage
articles.summary: Four Republican senators have signed on to a letter to the Defense Department’s inspector general expressing “grave concern” over Ukraine’s sudden loss of access to intelligence-sharing and high-speed Starlink data, which it needs to intercept Russian drones, and asked him to investigate whether senior Defense officials played a role. “We urgently request an Inspector General…
articles.body:
Four Republican senators have signed on to a letter to the Defense Department’s inspector general expressing “grave concern” over Ukraine’s sudden loss of access to intelligence-sharing and high-speed Starlink data, which it needs to intercept Russian drones, and asked him to investigate whether senior Defense officials played a role.

“We urgently request an Inspector General investigation into these incidents, including whether actions or decisions by the Department of Defense or its contractors contributed to these dangerous circumstances,” the Republican senators wrote in a bipartisan letter that was spearheaded by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

Republican Sens. Thom Tillis (N.C.), Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and John Cornyn (Texas) signed the letter to Platte Moring, the Pentagon’s inspector general.

They asked whether “any Department of Defense or other U.S. government officials directed, authorized, approved or had advance knowledge of changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements, warnings capabilities, or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine.”

Collins, a senior member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, is facing a competitive race for reelection this year in Maine, a state that former Vice President Kamala Harris carried in the last election.

Cornyn, who is retiring at the end of the year, is also a member of the Intelligence panel.

Democratic Sens. Dick Durbin (Ill.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Chris Coons (Del.) and Jack Reed (R.I.), the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, also signed the letter.

“We write with grave concern regarding reported disruptions to critical U.S.-supported communications and intelligence-sharing capabilities in Ukraine that have endangered American personnel and potentially compromised Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks,” the senators wrote.

They cited reports that restrictions imposed on data flowing through SpaceX’s Starlink terminals earlier this week disrupted the communications network supporting Ukraine’s uncrewed aerial vehicles and fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft.

They noted that the Ukrainian military on Oct. 14 reported restrictions to craft flying faster than 63 mph and that SpaceX reportedly acknowledged a service restriction on vehicles flying faster than 100 mph.

“These restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine’s ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure,” the senators wrote.

They also said they were “deeply concerned” by reports of disruptions affecting intelligence-sharing and threat-warning capabilities used by American personnel based in Ukraine.

They said that some American personnel experienced “serious difficulties reaching safety during Russian air raids” because of the so-called glitches and asked whether the disruptions were caused by changes in U.S. government policy.

“Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation,” the senators wrote.

Ukrainian officials said Wednesday that the disruptions in Ukrainian access to Starlink- and Starshield-provided data stemmed from decisions made in Washington.

Starshield is the military version of Starlink, which is owned by SpaceX, the commercial space company founded and led by Elon Musk.

Musk on Wednesday deflected blame over Ukraine losing critical access to Starshield by noting in a post on social media that the Pentagon operates its communications systems.

Musk explained that Starshield systems “are owned and controlled by the U.S. government” and emphasized “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” referring to the president of the United States.

The Republican and Democratic senators who wrote to the Pentagon inspector general warned that “any restrictions” on Ukraine’s ability to access Starshield data to operate its drones and military aircraft “raise serious questions about the Department of Defense’s contractual oversight and its responsibility to ensure continuity of essential services.”

They asked Moring to “immediately investigate” whether disruptions to intelligence sharing, threat warnings and other U.S.-supported capabilities made it tougher for American diplomatic, military and security personnel to reach shelter during Russian attacks.

They also want Moring to find out whether intelligence-sharing disruptions and Starlink restrictions are connected and whether they were the result of “deliberate policy decisions.”

They asked the inspector general to initiate an immediate investigation and provide written confirmation of its status no later than Nov. 1, two days before Election Day.

articles.title: Anthropic PAC splits Q3 donations down the middle
articles.summary: {beacon} Technology Technology The Big Story Anthropic PAC splits Q3 donations down the middle Anthropic’s corporate political action committee poured $161,000 into campaigns across the aisle last month, bringing their total third-quarter spending to more than $250,000, according to spending records first shared with The Hill. © Patrick Sison, Associated Press The employee-funded PAC,…
articles.body:
Anthropic PAC splits Q3 donations down the middle

Anthropic’s corporate political action committee poured $161,000 into campaigns across the aisle last month , bringing their total third-quarter spending to more than $250,000, according to spending records first shared with The Hill.

The employee-funded PAC, AnthroPAC , spent more than $255, 000 across the third quarter, marking the artificial intelligence firm’s latest push for political clout in Washington.

The party breakdown for Anthropic’s total third-quarter contributions was 50.6 percent for Republicans and 49.4 percent for Democrats.

Overall, AnthroPAC spent $130,000 on Republican campaigns and $125,500 on Democrats in the third quarter, according to spending records obtained by The Hill ahead of the monthly federal filing deadline next Tuesday.

September was the company’s biggest month for spending as the midterm election approaches. About $77,000 was spent in August, and $17,500 in July.

Recipients of the political donations include the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and various party-affiliated PACs.

Anthropic launched the employee-funded PAC in April, and it is overseen by a bipartisan board.

The donations are capped at $5,000 per person per year under federal law and will be publicly reported through Federal Election Commission filings.

articles.title: FDA advances peptide push to White House
articles.summary: Presented by Coalition to Strengthen America’s Healthcare {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story RFK Jr. advances peptide push The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) this week submitted a peptide “interim access policy” to the White House for review, according to a government filing, which would reportedly allow compounding pharmacies to temporarily produce and sell previously restricted…
articles.body:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) this week submitted a peptide “interim access policy” to the White House for review, according to a government filing, which would reportedly allow compounding pharmacies to temporarily produce and sell previously restricted peptides.

Such a move would let these peptides on the market while FDA develops permanent rules, according to the Associated Press, despite a lack of evidence supporting their purported benefits .

The FDA’s filing with the Office of Management and Budget did not give details on the policy, but it follows an agency advisory panel meeting this summer that voted to allow production of peptides to treat conditions like insomnia, obesity and wound healing.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. describes himself as “a big fan of peptides” and has promised action to expand access to them. Kennedy said compounding pharmacies must be allowed to sell peptides because Americans are using unsafe, “gray market” versions of these drugs made in China and other countries.

Pharmaceutical companies have brought several peptide drugs to market, including insulin. But the peptides the Health and Human Services Department (HHS) are interested in have not been tested or vetted by the FDA.

The FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted in July in favor of adding six peptides to the list of substances compounding pharmacies can make.

Those substances were among 14 that had previously been banned because of potential serious safety risks.

The votes were split nearly evenly among the committee, and the decision to vote in favor of adding the peptides to the list went against FDA scientists’ evaluations.

In briefing materials, agency researchers concluded that “based on the available data, there is a lack of evidence to make a conclusion on the effectiveness of BPC-157 for treating [ulcerative colitis]” and that current information “weighs against” adding it to the 503A compounding list.

Staffers came to the same conclusions for all six peptides the committee approved, finding there wasn’t enough evidence to support adding any of them to the permitted compoundable substances.

articles.body:
Pentagon’s school system director stepping down

The director of the Pentagon’s school system, Paul Craft, is resigning at the end of this month — less than eight months after being selected to lead the agency, a Defense official confirmed to The Hill Thursday.

The official said Craft, who stepped into the Department of Defense Education Activity’s (DoDEA) director role in early March, “ led efforts to reform ” the agency in “support of our military children and families.”

“Under his leadership, the DoWEA sharpened its focus on the fundamentals: strong classrooms, well-prepared teachers, transparent engagement with parents, and high academic standards for our military-connected students around the world,” the official said in a statement. “He led a comprehensive update to the DoWEA Blueprint for Continuous Improvement and helped realign the organization around the people it exists to serve: our students, parents, educators and military families.”

The official did not share why Craft, who began leading the DoDEA March 9 , is stepping down.

The agency did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

DoDEA is an education system that operates 160 schools in 11 countries, seven states and two U.S. territories for over 67,000 dependent children of U.S. military personnel and civilian staff.

Craft, a retired colonel in the Ohio Army National Guard, was picked after Beth Schiavino-Narvaez stepped down in early March. The Pentagon did not say at the time why Schiavino-Narvaez left the post.

Before Schiavino-Narvaez, the DoDEA was led by Thomas Brady, a retired colonel, from 2014 to 2024 .

“Craft’s work reduced unnecessary bureaucracy and maximize resource delivery to local school communities. During his tenure, Craft focused on supporting military families, recognizing the connection between family well-being and force readiness,” the Pentagon official said. “He understood that when parents trust the education their children receive, they can remain focused on their mission .”

The official said the Pentagon is “ grateful ” for Craft’s service to “ our military families and wishes him and his family well in their next chapter.”

articles.title: Can cooking for terrorists bar asylum? Supreme Court takes up unusual case with broader immigration stakes
articles.summary: A Nigerian man forced to cook for the Unknown Gunmen terrorist group is now at the center of a Supreme Court battle over asylum and material support.
articles.body: A Nigerian man forced to cook thousands of meals for the Unknown Gunmen, a militant group linked to political violence in Nigeria, is at the center of a Supreme Court showdown that could determine how broadly immigration authorities can apply a terrorism-related bar to asylum and how far the Trump administration can go in deporting immigrants accused of supporting terrorism. The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to hear the Trump administration's challenge to a ruling that overturned Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba's deportation order, setting up a legal battle over whether ordinary services provided to terrorist organizations, including cooking meals, can disqualify immigrants from receiving asylum even when those services are not directly connected to terrorist attacks. Ozurumba was deported to Nigeria in April 2025 while his appeal was pending. THE SUPREME COURT IS BACK; THESE FIVE CASES COULD RESHAPE AMERICAN LIFE At the center of the case is a provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act that bars certain immigrants who provide "material support" to terrorist organizations from receiving asylum. The law lists examples of prohibited assistance, including transportation, communications, housing, money, weapons and training, but it does not explicitly define what constitutes material support. "The biggest takeaway is that this is a case about who gets to draw the line on a law that affects national security," Bryce Poole, a senior legal fellow with Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital. "Congress wrote a broad rule, and the court interpreted it narrowly." The case also comes two years after the Supreme Court overturned Chevron deference, a legal doctrine that required judges to defer to federal agencies' reasonable interpretations of ambiguous laws. The 2024 ruling gave judges greater authority to decide what those laws mean. The 4th Circuit, in a 2-1 ruling, overturned Ozurumba's deportation order and sent the case back to the Board of Immigration Appeals. Judge James Wynn Jr., an Obama appointee, wrote the majority opinion, joined by Judge Nicole Berner, a Biden appointee. The judges concluded that, although Ozurumba prepared thousands of meals for the group's leaders, his cooking did not provide resources that could be directly used or readily redirected toward terrorist operations. Although Ozurumba said he was forced to cook under threat of violence, the 4th Circuit did not decide whether the law contains an exception for assistance provided under duress, an issue the court previously addressed in a 2012 ruling that relied on Chevron deference. Instead, the majority found that his cooking for the terrorist organization did not qualify as "material support" that would bar him from asylum, leaving the separate duress question unresolved. The Trump administration argued that the 4th Circuit interpreted the law too narrowly, insisting that even ordinary services such as cooking meals can help sustain a terrorist organization and free its members to carry out attacks. "Because he's cooking the meals, one of the armed guards doesn't have to cook the meals and can be an armed guard," Poole said. "That's one guard who doesn't have to come in off guard duty to cook meals, or that's one bomb maker who doesn't have to stop making bombs to go cook meals, because all this stuff is fungible." Ozurumba said he initially agreed to work as a chef at a "rural camp," preparing three meals a day for 15 to 17 leaders. He later learned the camp belonged to the Unknown Gunmen. An immigration judge determined that the Unknown Gunmen qualified as a "Tier III" terrorist organization under federal immigration law, even though the State Department had not formally designated the group as one. Ozurumba said armed guards prevented him from leaving. According to court records, he cooked for the group's leaders for roughly six months, including three months without pay, before escaping during a trip into town to buy groceries. STATE'S LARGEST MOSQUE LEADER’S DEPORTATION FIGHT TAKES DRAMATIC TURN AS TRUMP ADMIN SCORES MAJOR WIN Ozurumba said members of the Unknown Gunmen continued threatening and attacking him after his escape, prompting him to flee Nigeria for Venezuela and eventually the United States. He crossed the southern border without valid entry documents in July 2023 during the Biden administration and surrendered to Border Patrol agents. An immigration judge denied Ozurumba's asylum request and ordered his deportation, a decision upheld by the Board of Immigration Appeals after finding that his cooking violated the federal material-support rule. The 4th Circuit later rejected that interpretation and sent the case back to the immigration board. Judge Julius Richardson disagreed with the majority, arguing in his dissent that cooking thousands of meals for terrorist leaders freed them to focus on their organization's goals and therefore constituted material support. "Ozurumba did not run a hot dog stand that the Unknown Gunmen happened to stop by once or twice," Richardson wrote. "Rather, he acted as a private chef, providing three meals a day for over a dozen leaders of a terrorist organization — for months." Hans von Spakovsky, a legal expert with Advancing American Freedom, also argued that the majority misinterpreted the law. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "The idea that providing over 8,000 meals for the leaders of a terrorist organization and its members is not 'material' defies common sense," von Spakovsky told Fox News Digital. "Richardson correctly cites Napoleon’s famous quote that an 'army marches on its stomach.' CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Other federal appeals courts have all held that providing food and shelter, even if unconnected to a specific terrorist event, constitutes material support within the statute," von Spakovsky continued. "And doing so under duress, even if true, is not an excuse under the statute to avoid removal." Even if the Supreme Court rules in his favor, a victory would not automatically grant him asylum or guarantee his return to the United States. His case would still need to be reconsidered by immigration authorities. The 4th Circuit previously declined to order the government to bring him back, instead leaving it up to officials to decide whether his presence in the U.S. would be necessary for further proceedings.
